paragraphs: The paper builds a computer model of olfactory cortex using anatomical and physiological evidence. Its purpose is to connect the organization of this brain region with its ability to store and retrieve odor information. The simulation reproduces patterns of activity across both space and time under several conditions.

Learning combines a simple Hebbian rule with the activity dynamics produced by the modeled circuitry. Representations emerge through sparse connections that spread signals to many neurons and gather signals from many others. The simulations show that different input patterns can acquire distinct cortical representations while causing little interference with previously stored representations.

After learning, an incomplete version of an input can recover its fuller cortical representation. The model also allows the overlap between representations to change: similar inputs can become more distinguishable, while dissimilar inputs can acquire overlapping representations. These results connect reliable retrieval with flexible classification. The proposed circuitry can support both remembering an odor from partial evidence and adjusting which odors are treated as related.
neurips-1987-a-computer-simulation-of-ol.tldr: A biologically grounded olfactory-cortex simulation learns odor representations that support partial-input recall and flexible discrimination.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a practical obstacle in analog neural hardware: lateral inhibition circuits built with local resistive grids can spontaneously oscillate. These unwanted oscillations can make a circuit unusable. Designing against them is difficult when the grid contains resistances and capacitances whose values are uncertain or not explicitly modeled.

The proposed design method guarantees stability using mathematical analysis based on Tellegen's theorem and Popov multipliers from control theory. Its central practical feature is that the stability criteria can be checked locally. Designers use measured frequency responses of individual cells without having to analyze the complete interconnected circuit as one large system.

The analysis remains applicable even when the resistive interconnection grid contains unmodeled parasitic resistances and capacitances. This makes the guarantee useful for physical implementations, where the circuit includes more than its deliberately designed elements. The contribution is therefore both theoretical and operational: it turns a whole-network stability problem into measurable cell-level criteria while accounting for uncertainty in the connecting grid.
neurips-1987-a-method-for-the-design-of-.tldr: Local measurements of individual circuit cells can guarantee stable lateral inhibition despite unknown resistive-grid parasitics.

paragraphs: The paper treats classification as an error-correction problem. An input begins as a vector of measured features, but the network transforms it into an internal representation in a code space. Classification then consists of decoding that representation as a noisy codeword to identify the corresponding class.

This separates the description of an input from the representation used to decide its class. Coding theory supplies the structure for the second stage: the decoder corrects discrepancies in the internal code instead of assigning a class directly from the original features. The paper identifies Hadamard matrix codes and maximal length sequence codes as two choices that give high performance.

The stated capacity result is that an N-neuron classifier can store a number of classes proportional to N. The authors report that this is substantially more than a Hopfield-type memory can provide when used as a classifier. The significance is a direct connection between class capacity and code design: the internal representation is an essential part of how the network performs classification.
neurips-1987-a-neural-network-classifier.tldr: The classifier maps inputs into error-correcting codes, supporting a class count that grows linearly with neuron count.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to construct neural networks for pattern classification around an ordered sequence of attributes. The network gives attention first to the attributes regarded as most important, then extracts less important ones later. Classification is therefore organized around a ranking of the information available in a pattern.

The sequence is central to the proposal. Attributes do not all receive the same position in the decision process: their relative importance determines when they are considered. This provides a concrete interpretation of sequential decision making in the paper, namely arranging the examination of a pattern so that its more important characteristics come earlier.

The second stated feature concerns training. The authors use information as the training measure instead of error, linking the learning procedure to the informative content of pattern attributes. Together, these choices describe a classifier whose construction emphasizes both what to examine and the order in which to examine it. The contribution presented in the abstract is this proposed learning scheme and its organizing principles.
neurips-1987-a-novel-net-that-learns-seq.tldr: The proposed classifier examines attributes in importance order and trains using an information measure rather than error.

paragraphs: The paper develops a neural network for decoding convolutional codes and for more general finite impulse response signal deconvolution problems. Its computation optimizes a function related to log likelihood, connecting the network's evolving state with the task of finding a plausible explanation for a received signal.

The architecture consists of cooperating Grossberg subnets with an on-center, off-surround organization. Connections run only between neighboring subnets. This local structure matters for implementation because it avoids requiring every part of the network to communicate directly with every other part. The authors identify it as a type of architecture suited to VLSI hardware.

The paper reports analytical and experimental results concerning convergence and stability, addressing how the network behaves as its computation unfolds. It also describes how the structure can distribute the representation of data items while supporting fault tolerance and replacement of faulty units. The contribution brings together a signal-processing objective, local interconnections, and a representation designed to accommodate failures in individual components.
neurips-1987-a-trellis-structured-neural.tldr: A network of locally connected subnets supports likelihood-related signal decoding, with analyses of stability and convergence.

paragraphs: The paper starts from an observation about motion processing in the blowfly visual system. Neural units in a high-level optic ganglion change their temporal response according to object speed: over a wide range, their time constants are approximately inversely proportional to velocity. Faster motion therefore corresponds to shorter response times.

The authors implement a two-dimensional adaptive heterodyne filter in a computer simulation. The model is designed to account for this stimulus-dependent adjustment of temporal behavior. Its key connection to the biological observation is that the processing timescale adapts to the moving input, allowing the modeled response to vary with the speed being processed.

The simulations show improved imaging of moving patterns at high velocities when this adaptive procedure is applied. The result links a measured property of the fly's visual system to a useful image-processing method. The paper's contribution is both an account of adaptive neural timing and a demonstration that incorporating such timing into a filter can improve the handling of rapidly moving patterns.
neurips-1987-an-adaptive-and-heterodyne-.tldr: A simulated adaptive heterodyne filter models speed-dependent fly visual responses and improves imaging of rapidly moving patterns.

paragraphs: The paper compares the information capacity of Kanerva's Sparse Distributed Memory with that of Hopfield-type networks. Its focus is the total information stored in relation to the number of network connections. This provides a common resource measure for comparing memories with different organizations.

Under the approximations used in the analysis, stored information grows proportionally to connection count. The proportionality constant is the same for the memory models considered, including different model orders. The authors check the approximations numerically. The result makes the assumptions important: the shared capacity relationship is a conclusion of this approximate analysis.

The same framework also addresses temporal storage. It shows that Sparse Distributed Memory can hold sequences of patterns distributed across space and time. Adding delayed connections permits retrieval of temporal patterns that depend on context, while a small modification permits storage of correlated patterns. The paper thus connects a comparison of storage efficiency with extensions that handle relationships among memories, both across a sequence and among similar stored patterns.
neurips-1987-capacity-for-patterns-and-s.tldr: An approximate analysis finds shared information-per-connection scaling for SDM and Hopfield-type memories and extends SDM to temporal patterns.

paragraphs: The paper studies how preferred visual orientations are arranged across monkey primary visual cortex. The organization must satisfy two competing observations: nearby cells tend to prefer similar orientations, yet a small region contains cells preferring many different orientations. A useful model must explain local similarity together with local diversity.

Several orientation-map models meet both requirements, so those observations alone do not distinguish their spatial organization. The paper finds differences in the spacing and topological index of their singularities. These are features of how the orientation pattern is organized around special locations in the map, rather than simply which orientations are present.

To connect these structural differences with observations, the authors compare the models against published experimental results using the rate at which preferred orientation changes across the cortex. This gives the comparison a measurable spatial criterion. The contribution is a way to distinguish otherwise plausible maps by examining how rapidly orientation preferences vary and how the map's singularities organize that variation.
neurips-1987-centric-models-of-the-orien.tldr: The paper compares cortical orientation-map models through their singularities and the spatial rate of orientation change.

paragraphs: The paper places neural-like processing systems in relation to established ways of describing computation. It focuses on simple systems based on multiple context and connects them with production systems, fixed-length sequence prediction, finite-state machines, and Turing machines. Its central task is to clarify relationships among these different computational formalisms.

The motivation is renewed interest in connectionist approaches, partly driven by dissatisfaction with symbolic manipulation and by the prospect of massively parallel hardware. Relating neural-like systems to familiar formalisms gives that interest a more concrete foundation: it makes their computational organization discussable in terms already used for rules, sequences, and machines.

The paper also reinterprets earlier sequence-prediction results through these connections. This makes its contribution conceptual as well as retrospective. Work described in the language of neural networks can be examined alongside work expressed in other computational languages. The resulting perspective helps explain how multiple-context systems fit into a broader study of computation and how earlier results bear on renewed interest in connectionist processing.
neurips-1987-connecting-to-the-past-d64f.tldr: The paper relates multiple-context neural systems to established computational formalisms and reinterprets earlier sequence-prediction results.

paragraphs: CYCLES is a simulation program for studying neural networks whose connections contain loops. Its focus is oscillatory behavior: activity that evolves through repeated circulation along cyclic paths. The program gives researchers a graphical interface for building networks, running them, and inspecting the behavior produced by their connectivity.

The authors implemented the tool on the Texas Instruments Explorer/Odyssey system and used it to investigate several kinds of cycles. These include cycles activated at one or more points, cycles that cannot be interrupted, cycles with different path lengths, and cycles that interact. The variety makes network timing and interaction explicit subjects of experimentation.

Interacting cycles receive particular attention because they can implement goal processing that depends on time. This connects the study of recurring neural activity with a computational purpose beyond simply observing oscillations. The paper's contribution combines a working research interface with experiments on cyclic structures, making it possible to construct and examine networks in which the timing of activity is part of the computation.
neurips-1987-cycles-a-simulation-tool-fo.tldr: CYCLES provides a graphical simulation environment for exploring oscillatory neural circuits and time-dependent goal processing.

paragraphs: The paper constructs neural networks whose responses remain unchanged under specified geometric transformations of the input. It derives constraints on connection weights for translation, rotation, scaling, and several combinations. The aim is to make invariance a property of the network's structure rather than something dependent on a particular learned solution.

Each unit must satisfy the relevant weight constraints. Within the resulting architecture, invariant behavior is maintained regardless of the particular permitted weight values, the learning rule, or the form of the network's nonlinearities. This separates the guarantee of geometric invariance from the choice of how the network is trained.

The authors explain why higher-order networks matter for this construction. A first-order network may achieve only a trivial invariant response, such as using the average input for translation invariance. Higher-order networks can retain useful functionality while satisfying the invariance requirements. Alongside the derivations, the paper reports simulation studies. The central contribution is an architectural route to preserving geometric consistency without restricting the network to such simple invariant summaries.
neurips-1987-encoding-geometric-invarian.tldr: Weight constraints build geometric invariance into higher-order networks independently of the learning rule and permitted weight values.

paragraphs: The paper examines neural networks as tools for accurate numerical computation. It challenges the view that their main strength must be approximate qualitative reasoning by presenting applications in which their numerical accuracy exceeds that of conventional techniques. Prediction of future values in a chaotic time series is a central example.

To explain this behavior, the authors analyze networks geometrically as function approximators. They show that a large class of mappings between real-valued vector spaces can be accurately approximated by a backpropagation network with two hidden layers. The learned mapping provides a mathematical account of how a network transforms inputs into outputs.

The paper interprets signal-processing applications through interpolation and symbol-processing applications through extrapolation. This connects apparently different uses of neural networks to familiar operations on an approximated function. The stated accuracy results concern particular applications, while the broader contribution is an explanatory framework: network behavior can be understood through the geometry of the functions it represents and its relationship to established function-approximation methods.
neurips-1987-how-neural-nets-work-d41a66.tldr: The paper explains accurate neural computation through function approximation, including two-hidden-layer networks and chaotic time-series prediction.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how catfish use taste to locate and pursue food. It treats the gustatory system as a goal-directed processing architecture that continually interacts with its environment. Anatomical analysis identifies reticular neurons in the medullary brainstem as a link between taste-related sensory signals and spinal motor outputs.

Electrophysiological observations suggest that these neurons combine selected patterns of sensory input across space and time. The incoming signals pass through a rapidly adapting peripheral filter. According to the abstract, a sustained response occurs only when stimulus concentration continues increasing, tying ongoing sensory activity to how the chemical signal changes during tracking.

The authors interpret the connectivity and response patterns as evidence for a possible gustation-seeking function of reticulospinal cells. Once the direction of a stimulus source has been computed, these cells may help maintain pursuit through continuing environmental feedback. The proposed mechanism connects sensory filtering, neural integration, and movement, explaining how a processing pipeline could remain responsive while the animal is actively seeking food.
neurips-1987-how-the-catfish-tracks-its-.tldr: Anatomical and physiological evidence suggests brainstem neurons help catfish sustain food tracking through taste-driven sensory feedback.

paragraphs: The paper addresses communication when simulating neural networks on massively parallel SIMD machines. These machines can contain many processing elements operating under a shared instruction scheme, making them attractive for neural simulation. Their difficulty is supporting the varied connections that a general neural network may require.

The proposed system centers on an algorithm for forming arbitrary connections between simulated neurons. It supports rapid addition of new connections, includes error recovery, and works across a variety of network topologies. These features address the connectivity layer needed to make a parallel machine useful for networks with different structures.

Simulations and an implementation on the Connection Machine indicate that time and space requirements scale with the product of two quantities: average connections per neuron and the diameter of the interconnection network. This links the cost of supporting neural communication to both connection density and the extent of the underlying communication structure. The contribution is a practical connection mechanism together with an account of the factors governing its resource requirements.
neurips-1987-introduction-to-a-system-fo.tldr: A connection algorithm enables arbitrary neural wiring on SIMD hardware, with resource costs tied to connectivity and network diameter.

paragraphs: The paper learns a lightness algorithm from examples pairing image irradiance with desired surface reflectance. The task is to separate properties of surfaces from the illumination falling on them in a Mondrian world. Rather than specifying the full transformation directly, the authors synthesize it using optimal linear estimation.

The method assumes that the mapping from input to output is linear. The resulting algorithm is approximately equivalent to center-surround filtering applied separately within chromatic channels, and it resembles a lightness algorithm proposed by Land. This connects the learned transformation with a recognizable form of visual filtering.

The authors compare this approach with other learning methods, including backpropagation, and report no significantly different or better lightness algorithm in the Mondrian setting. Both linear estimation and backpropagation produce simultaneous brightness contrast effects. The result shows that the linearity assumption can be sufficient for this task. The authors also identify a class of early-vision algorithms satisfying that assumption as candidates for similar synthesis from examples.
neurips-1987-learning-a-color-algorithm-.tldr: Linear estimation learns a center-surround-like lightness algorithm that performs comparably to backpropagation in a Mondrian world.

paragraphs: MURPHY connects a camera and robot arm through a neural architecture that learns from the arm's own movement. By exploring a small representative sample of a billion possible joint configurations, it learns relationships between joint positions and the visual scene. The relationships can be used in both directions.

In the forward direction, the internal model predicts visual consequences from arm configurations. This lets MURPHY envision sequences of actions for planning, including reaching for a visually presented object. In the reverse direction, it uses visual activity to guide its arm, allowing it to imitate activity occurring in the camera's view.

The learning method explicitly uses continuity in the relationship between visual space and joint space. With that structure, MURPHY learns nonlinear mappings using only one layer of adjustable weights. The significance is that the system's learned model supports both prediction and action selection, while the continuity of the task helps make learning possible from a limited sample of its many possible configurations.
neurips-1987-murphy-a-robot-that-learns-.tldr: MURPHY learns bidirectional relationships between arm positions and camera views to support action planning and imitation.

paragraphs: The paper examines a difficulty that remains even when a distributed memory has very high storage capacity. Pattern recognition can be underspecified by the features describing the environment. In that situation, the available descriptions do not support clean separation of all patterns into their classes, regardless of the memory's storage potential.

The authors review high-density memory systems and their network implementations, emphasizing developments with economical feedforward architectures. They also discuss a general learning algorithm and its application to separable point sets. This establishes the setting in which the memory can learn class distinctions supported by the supplied features.

The proposed extension addresses non-separable point sets by learning probability distributions. That changes what the system represents when the features leave class membership ambiguous: it learns a probabilistic description of the pattern environment. The contribution therefore connects high-capacity storage with the separate problem of uncertainty in classification. More storage enables larger applications, while distribution learning addresses ambiguity that additional storage alone cannot resolve.
neurips-1987-pattern-class-degeneracy-in.tldr: The paper extends high-density memory learning to represent probability distributions when available features cannot separate pattern classes.

paragraphs: The paper investigates abrupt qualitative changes observed in simulations of cortical subnetworks as important parameters vary. Such changes resemble phase transitions: crossing a critical parameter value changes the kind of collective behavior a network exhibits. The authors ask how this observation should be understood mathematically.

For analogous models built from infinite arrays, they demonstrate that phase transitions must exist. This gives a theoretical basis for transition-like behavior rather than relying solely on simulation observations. The infinite-array setting is central to that result because it supports the classical description of changes in steady-state behavior.

Related finite arrays require a different interpretation. They may lack classical steady-state phase transitions, yet still show distinct changes in metastable transient behavior as parameters cross critical values. In other words, the behavior before final settling can change qualitatively even without a classical transition in the steady state. The paper's contribution is to separate these two possibilities and show why transition-like dynamics can matter in finite neural models.
neurips-1987-phase-transitions-in-neural.tldr: Infinite neural arrays exhibit phase transitions, while finite counterparts can show critical changes in metastable transient behavior.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a network whose local state is a two-dimensional vector with fixed unit length. Because the length cannot change, variation in a unit's state is expressed through its direction. This gives the network a phase-like representation, reflected in the name phasor neural network.

The authors use associative memory as an application of this representation. They define memory networks within the phasor framework and analyze their performance. The application connects the proposed local variables to a concrete computational task: storing information in a network that can subsequently retrieve associated information.

The paper also identifies physical systems corresponding to the model, including biological networks of limit-cycle oscillators and optical resonators with a hologram in the feedback path. These examples connect the mathematical representation with systems whose behavior can be described through oscillation and phase. The contribution is a neural-network formulation centered on fixed-length vector states, together with an associative-memory application and possible physical realizations of the same modeling idea.
neurips-1987-phasor-neural-networks-9735.tldr: Phasor networks use unit-length two-dimensional states, with associative-memory applications and possible oscillator-based physical realizations.

paragraphs: The paper interprets neural-network information retrieval as maximum a posteriori estimation: the network computes the most probable value of unknown information. This places retrieval within a probabilistic framework and makes it possible to state explicitly which family of probability distributions a network can acquire.

Once that family is specified, learning can be described as a search for its most probable member. The same formulation also supports statistical tests of whether the environmental distribution belongs to the family. These are complementary questions: which available distribution best accounts for the information, and whether the network's available distributions include the one generating it.

The authors discuss applications to backpropagation and to Hopfield and Anderson networks. The framework therefore provides a shared language for analyzing different neural models. Its significance is that retrieval, learning, and representational suitability become connected statistical problems. A network's behavior can be assessed through both the estimate it computes and the range of distributions its model permits it to learn.
neurips-1987-probabilistic-characterizat.tldr: A probabilistic framework links neural retrieval, learning, and tests of whether a network can represent its environment's distribution.

paragraphs: The paper studies how coarse-coded symbol memories scale as the demands on them increase. These memories appear in neural models of symbol processing, so understanding their mathematical properties is necessary for assessing larger versions of those systems. The authors begin by defining their general structure.

The analysis derives relationships among three essential quantities: memory size, the size of the available symbol set, and storage capacity. These quantities describe different aspects of the problem. A system's physical memory, the vocabulary it must represent, and how much it can store must be considered together when reasoning about scale.

For one of the schemes, the calculated capacity agrees well with measurements from the working memory of DCPS, Touretzky and Hinton's distributed connectionist production system. This connects the mathematical analysis with an implemented symbol-processing model. The contribution is a framework for relating representation choices to storage requirements, backed by a capacity calculation that matches observed behavior in a concrete coarse-coded memory.
neurips-1987-scaling-properties-of-coars.tldr: The paper derives scaling relationships for coarse-coded symbol memories and checks one capacity prediction against DCPS measurements.

paragraphs: The paper extends error-propagation networks from fixed patterns to patterns that vary over time. In the static setting, a network learns a mapping between an input pattern and an output pattern. The dynamic setting makes a time-varying pattern itself the subject of the learned mapping, which is especially relevant to speech.

The authors explore three possible architectures for this extension. They apply dynamic networks to speech coding using a pair of networks: one encodes a sequence of speech data, and another decodes it. This creates a concrete task in which the learned transformation must support reconstruction of a signal unfolding over time.

The reported result is a better signal-to-noise ratio with dynamic networks than with static networks. That means the reconstructed speech signal has a stronger signal relative to noise under the reported comparison. The contribution is both an architectural generalization of error propagation and an application showing that treating speech as a dynamic pattern can improve coding quality.
neurips-1987-static-and-dynamic-error-pr.tldr: Dynamic error-propagation networks encode and decode speech sequences with a better signal-to-noise ratio than static networks.

paragraphs: The paper challenges the belief that the delta rule is guaranteed to train a network successfully whenever it has no hidden units. For classification tasks, that guarantee does not hold. The authors give explicit counterexamples showing two different ways the learning rule can fail, making the distinction between a simple architecture and reliable training concrete.

They then provide conditions under which gradient descent does successfully train networks without hidden units for two-category classification. The task assigns positive outputs to one finite set of input vectors and negative outputs to another. Assuming an odd output function allows the analysis to combine these requirements into a single positive-output condition on transformed training vectors.

This formulation makes successful classification a precise requirement on the weight vector, so training can be studied in relation to the set of weights that satisfy it. The paper also discusses extensions to hidden-unit networks and multiple categories. Its central contribution is a conditional account of training success grounded in counterexamples and sufficient conditions.
neurips-1987-strategies-for-teaching-lay.tldr: Counterexamples expose delta-rule failures, and sufficient conditions establish when gradient descent succeeds at two-category classification.

paragraphs: The paper proposes networks in which neurons communicate only through the timing of individual firing events. A received message says that another neuron fired, rather than carrying a numerical activation value. The authors identify implementation advantages in restricting communication to these time markers.

Each neuron fires regularly on its own. Interaction changes the schedule: a neighboring neuron's firing can advance or delay the next event. Together, the neurons form a global oscillator with several possible synchronizing attractors, meaning that the network can settle into different coordinated patterns of repeated activity.

Energy-minimization learning procedures can guide the network from arbitrary initial states toward oscillatory modes satisfying multidimensional constraints. This gives the timing dynamics a computational role: the relationships among firing events can encode a solution. Routing and scheduling are direct applications because they involve arranging events in sequences. The contribution is an architecture in which event timing serves simultaneously as the communication medium and the representation of an ordered computational result.
neurips-1987-synchronization-in-neural-n.tldr: Networks that communicate through firing times can synchronize into oscillatory patterns representing routing and scheduling solutions.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many words an associative memory can store while reliably retrieving them from imperfect addresses. Reliability is defined through a sphere of attraction: addresses within a specified Hamming distance of a stored address should recover its contents. Capacity is therefore tied to the fraction of address errors the memory must correct.

Using sphere-packing arguments, the authors establish an exponential upper growth rate as address length increases. The rate is one minus the binary entropy of the permitted error fraction. They show that Kanerva's memory can achieve this growth when its parameters are set optimally, and provide formulas for those settings.

The capacity definition concerns most address-and-data sequences in a probabilistic sense, because arbitrary sequences can create unavoidable conflicts, such as different contents assigned to the same address. Within that definition, the exponential result contrasts with the stated sublinear capacity growth of Hopfield memory. The significance is a capacity claim with both a specified retrieval tolerance and an explicit condition on parameter choice.
neurips-1987-the-capacity-of-the-kanerva.tldr: With optimal parameters, Kanerva memory achieves exponential capacity growth under a probabilistic, error-tolerant retrieval definition.
